stories.title: Google parent's revenue jumps 25% as homegrown AI chips take on Nvidia
stories.summary: Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported a 25% revenue increase as its internally developed AI chips gain traction as alternatives to Nvidia's dominant graphics processors in both internal workloads and external cloud offerings. The growth reflects successful commercialization of Google's custom silicon strategy across its advertising and cloud businesses.
stories.why_it_matters: Alphabet's revenue acceleration on homegrown silicon validates the multi-billion dollar capital commitment to custom chip development, pressuring AWS and Microsoft to accelerate their own silicon roadmaps or risk margin compression as Nvidia's premium pricing becomes unsustainable at hyperscale deployment volumes. The competitive dynamic shifts from Nvidia's CUDA ecosystem lock-in toward a fragmented landscape of proprietary silicon-software stacks, potentially complicating enterprise AI portability and increasing vendor-specific optimization costs.

stories.title: 200 neoclouds may face wipeout amid hesitant AI lending: Musk
stories.summary: Over 200 neoclouds might face demise or consolidation because lenders are reluctant to finance businesses that depend wholly on AI demand,” SpaceX CEO Elon Musk warned in an X post recently. “Debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,” Musk wrote. He […]
stories.title_zh: Musk 警告：200 家 neocloud 或因 AI 融资困难面临淘汰
stories.content:
Over 200 neoclouds might face demise or consolidation because lenders are reluctant to finance businesses that depend wholly on AI demand,” SpaceX CEO Elon Musk warned in an X post recently.

“Debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,” Musk wrote. He added that SpaceX is immune because it has Starlink which generates revenue outside of the AI business. Also, SpaceX has already in hand US$ 40 billion in debt financing.

This is consistent with an article published by <u>w.media</u> recently which predicted that in the event of the AI boom popping, “… what’s likely to happen is that strong hyperscalers and top facilities will continue expanding while highly leveraged neoclouds and speculative projects will struggle. Private credit, special-purpose vehicles or data center bonds will take the first hit but there likely won’t be a massive equity crash.”

Fortune recently wrote that “paying for AI infrastructure has strained Silicon Valley’s deepest pockets, with even Meta reporting negative US$2.1 billion in free cash flow last week as its spending on data centers and chips surged.”

The earlier <u>w.media</u> article had said, “The sheer size of the investment needed to keep the AI trajectory going is unprecedented and so extraordinary that questions since 2023 have been asked about when this supposed AI bubble would eventually pop.

“But instead of winding down because the promised revenue has not kept up with capital expenditure so far, the parties in the ecosystem have continued to pump relentless (some say ‘obscene’) amounts of cash into the AI ‘black hole’ (where cash disappears and continuously requires larger amounts to keep the hole from imploding).

“The amounts have reached such dizzying heights that even hyperscalers that were previously awash with cash now have to borrow to sustain the AI momentum. The Financial Times (FT) reported that since 2025, “hyperscalers have tapped the US$11.7 trillion US corporate debt market repeatedly, so much so that they have to begin raising debt in foreign currencies to broaden the investor pool.”

#### **“80pc will stop operating by 2030”**

 Fortune.com affirmed that by saying, “Neoclouds, firms that buy chips and then rent out GPU computing capacity for AI, borrow heavily to buy expensive Nvidia chips and build data centers, and then lease out that capacity to model developers.

“While hyperscalers like Google and Meta have other sources of revenue they can lean on to fuel their AI spending, neoclouds’ survival depends on appetite for compute. So if borrowing costs go up or customers cut spending, neoclouds will struggle to pay off their debts.”

Research firm Gartner predicted recently that cost pressure and lack of a differentiating business model will force 80 per cent of neoclouds to stop operating by 2030. “Data center owners need to make US$8.6 trillion in revenue to cover financing costs and capital spending, but enterprise and consumer AI revenue linked to those data centers is forecast at only US$3.6 trillion.” That’s a jaw-dropping US$5 trillion gap.

AI infrastructure is also competing with government debt and deficit financing for funding, creating a “shortage of capital” for the industry, opined an analyst. Additionally, hyperscalers are issuing debt and stock in record numbers with plans to raise more in future to fund their AI efforts.

CoreWeave however argued that lenders distinguish between speculative capacity and businesses with differentiated technology, creditworthy customers, contracted revenue and a record of delivering, as per its response to Fortune.

stories.title: Sim: Automotive, data centres, aerospace offer higher-value opportunities for steelmakers
stories.summary: SUBANG JAYA (Oct 29): Malaysia’s iron and steel industry can seize opportunities to shift to higher-value production by supplying the automotive, data centre, and aerospace sectors, Deputy Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Sim Tze Tzin said.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: Sim：汽车、data centre、航空航天为钢铁制造商提供更高价值机遇
stories.content:
SUBANG JAYA (Oct 29): Malaysia’s iron and steel industry can seize opportunities to shift to higher-value production by supplying the automotive, data centre, and aerospace sectors, Deputy Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Sim Tze Tzin said.

He said the industry was transforming beyond its traditional focus on construction and infrastructure, with high-technology sectors opening up new markets for domestic producers.

In the automotive sector, he said a new incentive mechanism (NCM) to be implemented next year would require carmakers seeking lower excise duties to deepen localisation, creating opportunities for domestic steelmakers to supply automotive-grade steel.

“If they want to enjoy our excise duty, lower excise duties, then they have to really, really go deep into localisation — a genuine localisation,” he told reporters at the 15th Malaysian Iron and Steel Industry Federation (Misif) Conference on the Status and Outlook of the Industry here on Thursday.

He said the mechanism, which will be announced soon, would cover all carmakers, including Japanese, Korean and Chinese brands.

Carmakers would need to increase local sourcing, including replacing imported steel with locally produced materials, he added.

He expressed hope that the move would open up the automotive market to domestic steelmakers, while stressing that the industry must invest in producing automotive-grade steel.

Sim said efforts to replace imported steel in locally manufactured cars had yet to take off seriously due to price competition and the investment required to meet higher safety standards.

Meanwhile, he said Malaysia’s position as a major data centre hub in Asia offered opportunities for the industry to supply products such as server racks, cables and wire harnesses.

He said an industry player had told him its company was moving into supplying server racks for data centres, describing the development positively.

In aerospace, he said Malaysia’s maintenance, repair and overhaul industry needs components that could let steelmakers pursue higher-margin business, even at lower volumes.

He cited a European company producing high-technology steel for aircraft structures as an example of how the industry could move into higher-value applications.

On government support, Sim said steelmakers seeking to invest in more complex production could receive further incentives.

“Several major industry players had already benefitted from government incentives, including pioneer status and investment tax allowances.

“But if they want to invest further for a higher complexity, the government will help in terms of further incentives for them,” he said.

He said the government’s goal was to help the domestic steel industry innovate and develop more complex products to meet demands from an increasingly high-technology market.

stories.title: AMD & Meta expand AI partnership with Helios systems
stories.summary: Meta is boosting the computing base for its frontier models with AMD hardware, while AMD will invest USD $1 billion in the equity offering.
stories.title_zh: AMD 与 Meta 以 Helios 系统扩展 AI 合作
stories.content:
Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Today)
AMD and Meta have expanded their strategic partnership across chips, systems, networking and software, with AMD's Helios rack-scale systems now running at Meta.

The work also includes support for Meta's AI models and infrastructure.

Under the arrangement, AMD's EPYC processors support the computing environments behind Meta's Muse AI agent, while AMD Instinct GPUs are used in Meta production systems for training, ranking and recommendation workloads. Meta has also installed initial Helios rack-scale systems for testing ahead of a wider deployment.

Meta has deployed millions of EPYC processors across multiple generations and is a lead customer for AMD's sixth-generation EPYC CPUs. The two companies are also working on future processor generations, including a platform referred to as Verano.

On the graphics side, Meta is described as an early definition customer for AMD's Instinct MI450 architecture. It will also deploy a custom Instinct GPU tailored to its workloads, while collaboration between the companies is feeding into future platforms, including the Instinct MI500 series and later rack-scale systems.

The partnership also extends into software. AMD has worked with Meta on ROCm through PyTorch so developers can use AMD GPUs from the outset. It also delivered Day-0 support for Meta's Muse Spark Open models on AMD Instinct GPUs, and for Muse Glimmer on AMD Ryzen AI PCs and AMD Radeon GPUs.

Beyond model support, the companies have worked together on large-scale AI training and on optimising recommendation models on AMD Instinct MI350X GPUs. The work has also included contributions to PyTorch, Triton and ROCm for broader developer use.

A financial element accompanies the engineering tie-up: AMD will invest USD $1 billion in Meta's equity offering.

### Scale of build-out

The announcement offers a clearer view of how Meta is spreading its AI infrastructure across multiple layers of hardware and software as it expands the computing base behind its frontier models and consumer services. It also underlines AMD's push to secure a bigger role in the data centres of the world's largest AI spenders.

Meta has been investing heavily in the infrastructure needed to train and run large AI models, and the latest arrangement shows it is using AMD technology not only for general server compute but also for AI acceleration, networking and full-system design. The two companies have aligned product roadmaps and engineering decisions around both current and future Meta workloads.

That alignment reflects a broader industry shift, as major cloud and platform companies seek closer influence over chip design and system architecture. For suppliers such as AMD, those ties can create long-term demand, but they also require significant co-design work and software support.

AMD framed the relationship with Meta as the product of several years of technical collaboration spanning EPYC processors, Instinct GPUs, Pensando networking and ROCm software. The partnership has now moved into integrated AI systems designed for deployment at gigawatt scale.

"Meta is a strategic partner for AMD, and we have built this partnership through years of deep technical collaboration - from EPYC processors powering Meta's infrastructure to Instinct GPUs and open software supporting its AI workloads," said Lisa Su, Chair and CEO, AMD. "With Helios now running at Meta, we are taking that partnership to a new scale in the superintelligence era. Together, we are building and deploying infrastructure at gigawatt scale and shaping future generations of silicon, software and systems to enable Meta's most ambitious superintelligence models and services."

Meta linked the partnership to the computing demands of its most advanced AI efforts.

"AMD has been a key partner in building out the compute that's running our frontier models," said Mark Zuckerberg, Founder and CEO, Meta. "We're making big investments in the computing power that will enable us to bring personal superintelligence to everyone, and AMD plays an important role in that."

stories.title: AirTrunk secures AUD $4.25 billion green loan for SYD3
stories.summary: AirTrunk has secured a AUD $4.25 billion green loan to finance its SYD3 expansion at its Western Sydney campus, with construction targeting low-carbon methodologies and completion by mid-2028. The facility is projected to support more than 10,000 jobs during its development and operational phases.
stories.why_it_matters: The green loan's scale—among Asia-Pacific's largest single data center financings—validates sustainable finance frameworks as viable for multi-billion dollar infrastructure, though scrutiny of 'green' claims will intensify given the fundamental energy intensity of AI workloads. stories.summary_zh: AirTrunk已获得42.5亿澳元的green loan，用于资助其Western Sydney园区的SYD3扩建，建设目标采用low-carbon methodology并于2028年中期完工。该设施预计在开发和运营阶段支持超过10,000个工作岗位。

stories.content:
Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Today)
AirTrunk has secured an AUD $4.25 billion green loan to expand its SYD3 data centre campus in Western Sydney, supporting continued development of one of its Australian sites.

The funding will add infrastructure for cloud, artificial intelligence and other digital services used by businesses, government and community organisations. The project is expected to support more than 10,000 jobs across construction, trades, engineering, logistics and safety.

The green loan includes margin adjustments, with any savings directed to AirTrunk's social impact programme. The programme supports charities focused on STEM education, digital equity, biodiversity and conservation, sustainable innovation and disaster relief.

### Jobs and suppliers

The SYD3 expansion is also expected to create work for contractors and suppliers in Western Sydney and elsewhere in Australia, including in steel and precast manufacturing, freight and logistics, civil works, and electrical and mechanical services.

AirTrunk said its wider supplier base reflects the scale of its regional spending. In FY26, it worked with 1,436 supplier entities across Asia-Pacific, including 615 in Australia, accounting for AUD $3.4 billion in supplier activity.

For the SYD3 project, AirTrunk is using a 25,000 square metre strategic buffer zone in Western Sydney to store, stage and pre-commission data centre equipment before delivery to the campus. It has also invested in dedicated time-charter vessels moving equipment through Port Botany and Port Kembla.

"SYD3 is a long-term investment in Western Sydney and Australia's digital capability, backed by the confidence of leading Australian and international banks. As the campus develops, it's building a regional ecosystem through active hiring, sustained project activity and strategic supply chain partnerships, creating opportunities for local workers, contractors and businesses while delivering infrastructure Australians increasingly rely on. The green financing also reflects our view that sustainability should be built into how digital infrastructure is funded and delivered. We're focused on responsible growth that creates lasting value for communities in the regions where we operate," said Tom Mackellar, Vice President, Origination & Market Expansion, AirTrunk.

AirTrunk said it would continue working with local contractors, suppliers and community partners as the site develops. It is also supporting apprenticeships, technical skills development, vocational education links and post-trade upskilling through work on a national skills advisory group.

### Australian footprint

SYD3 will add computing and storage capacity for cloud, AI and enterprise services. AirTrunk said its Australian platform now spans five campuses with more than 1.2GW of capacity.

To date, AirTrunk has invested more than AUD $12 billion across Australian projects and plans a further AUD $75 billion over the next decade. Following the new loan, its total committed debt financing globally stands at about AUD $38.4 billion, including more than AUD $19.8 billion across Australian projects.

The financing is linked to AirTrunk's target of reaching net zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 2030. The approach includes energy efficiency measures, renewable energy matching and lower-carbon technologies, alongside efforts to reduce Scope 3 emissions through lower embodied carbon in new builds.

At the SYD3 campus, construction measures include lower-carbon steel and concrete, as well as a target to divert at least 90 per cent of non-hazardous construction waste from landfill. Construction of the expansion is under way, led by A W Edwards, with completion expected by mid-2028.

### Lender group

A consortium of 32 domestic and international financial institutions backed the facility, making it one of the largest lending groups assembled for a data centre financing in Australia. Fourteen banks underwrote the loan: Banco Santander, BNP Paribas, Crédit Agricole Corporate and Investment Bank, DBS Bank, Deutsche Bank, ING, Mizuho Bank, MUFG Bank, National Australia Bank, Royal Bank of Canada, Société Générale, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, HSBC and United Overseas Bank.

The Green Loan Coordinators were Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, HSBC and United Overseas Bank. Legal advisers on the transaction were King & Wood Mallesons for the borrower and Gilbert + Tobin for the lenders.

The size of the lender group highlights strong bank appetite for digital infrastructure financing in Australia as developers expand capacity to meet rising demand for data storage and computing. The project will add infrastructure increasingly used every day by Australian businesses, governments and communities.

stories.content:
NEW YORK/BENGALURU (Oct 28): Marvell Technology is in advanced talks to buy data-centre optics maker Lumentum Holdings, with a deal potentially set to be announced as soon as next week, a source familiar with the matter told *Reuters* on Wednesday.

Marvell and Lumentum did not immediately respond to *Reuters* requests for comment.

Lumentum makes optical components used in communications networks and data centres, areas that have attracted growing investor interest as AI workloads drive demand for faster data transmission.

Marvell has emerged as one of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI spending boom, with its shares nearly tripling this year as demand for its custom AI chips and networking products surged.

The potential acquisition would further Marvell's push into optical technologies used in AI infrastructure, a strategy that Bernstein analysts said was reinforced by the company's acquisition of photonics firm Celestial AI in a US$3.25 billion deal announced late last year.

Marvell raised its fiscal 2028 revenue forecast earlier this month to US$20 billion from US$15 billion, citing strong demand for its custom AI chips and networking products used in data centres.

While Marvell had about US$3.92 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of its latest quarter, Bernstein analysts said an acquisition of that size would likely require additional financing and could present integration challenges.

Shares of Lumentum, which has a market value of roughly US$83 billion, rose about 9% in extended trading following news of the discussions, first reported by *Bloomberg News*. Marvell shares fell more than 8%.

stories.content:
Australian water infrastructure company coNEXA will invest AU$250 million to expand its AquaNet recycled water network in Western Sydney, supplying up to 16 million litres of recycled water a day from its Fairfield recycled water plant to NextDC’s S4 Sydney data centre at Horsley Park.

Construction is scheduled to begin in November, with the first water expected to flow in late 2027. The project has received approval from the NSW Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal (IPART) and will be funded entirely by the private sector, according to coNEXA.

The company said the connection is believed to be the largest recycled water supply arrangement for a data centre in Australia. It will enable up to 5.8 billion litres of water a year that would otherwise be discharged to the ocean to be reused, while diverting wastewater equivalent to the output of up to 35,000 homes from a constrained sewerage network.

NextDC’s S4 Sydney campus, being developed at Horsley Park, is designed for up to 365MW of IT capacity and is targeting Tier IV certification, according to the company.

“Data centres are essential to a thriving digital economy, and with that comes a responsibility to use resources carefully. Cooling S4 Sydney with AquaNet’s recycled water puts that responsibility into operation,” said Jeff Van Zetten, NextDC’s chief engineering and design officer.

The operator said recycled water would support cooling designs requiring less power. S4 Sydney is designed to achieve a power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.125 at full IT load, which the company says is more than 25 percent below the 2026 global average reported by the Uptime Institute.

“This is exactly the type of project we envisioned when we released the NSW Data Centre Guidelines,” said NSW Minister for Water Rose Jackson. “Instead of sending billions of litres out to sea each year, we’re putting that water to productive use and building infrastructure that can support communities and industry for decades to come.”

### Recycled water as data centre infrastructure

The AquaNet project is part of coNEXA’s strategy to expand private-sector water infrastructure alongside data centre development, reducing reliance on drinking water and easing pressure on existing wastewater and water supply systems.

The company’s existing AquaNet network, developed after the Millennium Drought, has supplied recycled water to Western Sydney businesses and industry since 2011. In its submission to the NSW Legislative Council’s inquiry into data centres, coNEXA said the network can provide up to 25 million litres a day of recycled water for industrial use.

The company argued that water infrastructure planning should be integrated into data centre development strategies rather than treated as a separate issue. It said recycled and other non-potable water should play a larger role in cooling, particularly as large facilities increase demand for both electricity and water.

The submission stated that water-based cooling can reduce electricity demand compared with air-based alternatives, while recycled water can reduce competition with household drinking water supplies. It also said that although State Significant Development approvals frequently reference recycled water for cooling, there is currently “little to no” enabling infrastructure in place to deliver it at scale.

### Longer-term framework

coNEXA called on the NSW Government to encourage regulated utilities to work with licensed private water infrastructure providers, collaborate on solutions for other data centre hotspots, and initiate a longer-term framework for clearer collaboration pathways between regulated utilities and private water providers. It argued that privately funded, designed, built and operated infrastructure could accelerate delivery while reducing the burden on government capital programmes.

In its submission, coNEXA said water infrastructure needs to be planned and delivered alongside data centre developments to give investors greater certainty over supply and timing.

“NSW has set a clear direction for how the State can sustainably and responsibly host data centres, and recycled water is a key part of it,” said coNEXA CEO Kurt Dahl. “NextDC’s commitment to S4 Sydney unlocks the scale and demand to build the first stage of a network that will serve more of Western Sydney industry and the community over time.”

The network expansion could also create opportunities for other industrial users and local councils, including supplying recycled water for irrigation of public open spaces during dry weather and water restrictions. coNEXA said the project would support up to 200 construction jobs, alongside ongoing roles.

stories.summary: Enterprises are moving from global-by-default systems to regional architectures due to tightening AI regulation and data sovereignty requirements. Nearly 60 per cent of AI leaders cite cross-border data restrictions as a major challenge. This shift impacts how and where software is deployed.
stories.title_zh: AI主权推动企业转向regional infrastructure
stories.content:
AI regulation and data sovereignty requirements are reshaping enterprise infrastructure, driving organisations away from global-by-default systems towards regional architectures, according to Kevin Cochrane, Chief Marketing Officer at Vultr.Governments and regulators globally are demanding greater transparency on AI systems, data use, and infrastructure access. This has created overlapping rules that enterprises must navigate, with nearly 60 per cent of AI leaders citing cross-border data restrictions as a major challenge.
### Regulation as an Architectural Concern

Tightening regulation is changing software deployment, with legislation such as the EU AI Act and GDPR affecting data storage and usage. An AI system in the UK may face different requirements than an identical one in the US or Europe, even if based on the same model.Compliance can no longer be an afterthought, as the geographical placement of compute and inference environments are now fundamental architectural considerations. A single global deployment may no longer be viable.Sovereignty extends beyond data residency to include where models are hosted and where inference occurs. This is critical because AI often involves data passing through multiple components, requiring enterprises to track processing locations across the entire AI environment.
### The Regional Model

Building a new technology stack for each region is not feasible due to cost and consistency issues. Instead, enterprises are adopting a regional model with central control but local deployment. This allows engineering teams to maintain common policies while running workloads in designated regional environments, such as a UK cluster serving UK customers.This approach helps meet regulatory requirements, simplifies processes, and reduces costs. It allows organisations to choose where workloads run and where data is processed and stored, with evidence of adherence to local regulations.
### Making the Shift

Engineering teams must classify workloads based on data sensitivity, regulatory exposure, and business purpose, as not all workloads require the same regional consideration. Deployment pipelines should ensure workloads run in protected regional nodes with region-specific controls covering backup models, access, and compute.Auditability must be built into platforms to provide insight into model usage, inference location, and system access. These records support ongoing compliance oversight. Organisations must also test and update AI systems across regions to maintain compliance as regulations evolve.The next generation of AI infrastructure is being shaped by regional requirements rather than universal deployment. This model also helps manage costs and improve performance by keeping inference close to the edge, simplifying workloads.

# AI sovereignty drives enterprise shift to regional infrastructure

Enterprises are moving from global-by-default systems to regional architectures due to tightening AI regulation and data sovereignty requirements. Nearly 60 per cent of AI leaders cite cross-border data restrictions as a major challenge. This shift impacts how and where software is deployed.

- Published On Oct 29, 2026 at 07:46 AM IST

## Highlights

stories.title: Samsung sees AI chip shortage worsening, keeps investors in suspense on returns
stories.summary: The firm reports an operating profit of 107.4 trillion won for the July-to-September period
stories.title_zh: Samsung称AI芯片短缺加剧，回报问题令投资者悬心
stories.content:
The firm reports an operating profit of 107.4 trillion won for the July-to-September period

\[SEOUL\] Samsung Electronics posted a 15 times jump in quarterly chip profit on Thursday (Oct 29), powered by the artificial intelligence boom, but its shares tumbled as investors balked at a lack of fresh shareholder-return plans and an outlook that lagged rival SK Hynix’s.

Samsung shareholders’ hopes were up as SK Hynix on Wednesday reported better-than-expected earnings and an upbeat outlook while spelling out plans to return about US$75 billion to shareholders in 2026.

“SK Hynix did quite a lot more than expected yesterday ... it went beyond market expectations, but Samsung Electronics hasn’t really changed anything from the guidance it gave before,” said Lee Min-hee, analyst at BNK Investment & Securities.

SK Hynix said on Wednesday its dynamic random-access memory and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips were sold out through 2029 and the chip shortage would persist to 2030, helping ease market concerns that AI-driven chip earnings could lose momentum.

Samsung said its HBM supply has been sold out for 2027, with key customers requesting more of the key chips used in AI data centres, and gave a more conservative view than SK Hynix on how long the supply gap would last.

“In 2027, the (memory) business expects AI infrastructure capital expenditure to reach a historic level as the AI ecosystem expands,” it said in a statement.

“Increasing AI-driven demand will far exceed the industry supply in comparison with 2026.”

Samsung said the chip market is expected to remain tight through 2028, saying it will take time to build new fabrication plants despite a sharp increase in capital spending for its chip division in 2027, after a 62 per cent jump to 76.8 trillion won in 2026.

Samsung reported operating profit of 107.4 trillion won (US$80 billion) for the July-to-September period, in line with its estimate and up from 12.2 trillion won a year earlier.

Its semiconductor operating profit jumped to 106.5 trillion won, accounting for almost all of the group’s total profit, but that was slightly short of analysts’ estimate of 107.3 trillion won, according to LSEG.

Its shares opened higher then reversed course, falling as much as 6.2 per cent in morning trade, while SK Hynix rose 0.7 per cent.

“Samsung’s decline was likely attributable to its outlook on how long the memory shortage would last, which came across as marginally less bullish than SK Hynix’s commentary yesterday,” said Jing Jie Yu, an analyst at Morningstar.

## January decision on returns

The company previously said 2026’s shareholder returns would total between 90 trillion and 110 trillion won including 30 trillion won in third-quarter dividends.

On Thursday, it said it would finalise its next shareholder return policy in January.

“The market appeared to expect an additional buyback and/or dividend announcement, but the company deferred the decision until late January, potentially disappointing near-term expectations,” CLSA senior analyst Sanjeev Rana said.

While demand for AI chips is expected to remain resilient, concerns about financing for AI infrastructure and rising competition from China have weighed on chip stocks in recent months.

Google parent Alphabet reported on Wednesday a massive acceleration in cash burn as it poured resources into building out AI.

## New long-term customers

The pace of memory chip price gains is slowing as chipmakers sign more long-term supply contracts and higher chip prices weigh on demand from smartphone and personal computer makers.

Samsung said it has signed long-term supply contracts with 10 major customers and is in talks with another 10, aiming for such agreements to account for 60 to 70 per cent of its total production capacity by 2030.

It is expanding long-term sales beyond AI-related firms, such as hyperscalers, to include mobile and automotive customers, it said.

Analysts said Samsung’s foundry business remained at a loss, weighing on its chip division earnings.

However, Samsung said its foundry business experienced a notable revenue improvement on sales of the logic die for HBM chips and order wins in advanced two-nanometer chips from hyperscalers and other AI customers.

It will start mass production in 2027 at its Taylor plant in Texas, making chips for Tesla, while considering building a new fab to meet demand for advanced, two-nano chips.

Higher memory chip costs shrank margins in Samsung’s mobile business, which fell to a loss of 800 billion won. REUTERS

stories.title: How Australia's data centre boom could reshape regional economies
stories.summary: Australia's data center expansion is increasingly shifting toward regional locations outside the major capital cities of Sydney, Melbourne, and Brisbane, driven by availability of power, land, and connectivity. These emerging markets present both substantial development opportunities and significant infrastructure challenges for operators and local communities.
stories.why_it_matters: Regional migration threatens to fragment Australia's data center market from three dominant metro hubs into a dispersed network of smaller facilities, complicating interconnection economics and potentially degrading latency for financial services and real-time applications that remain Sydney-centric. For regional economies, the influx represents transformative employment but also strains local power grids and water systems designed for agricultural rather than industrial loads, creating political friction if infrastructure upgrades are perceived as subsidizing foreign technology capital at community expense.
stories.title_zh: 澳大利亚数据中心热潮如何重塑区域经济
stories.summary_zh: 澳大利亚的data center扩张正越来越多地转向Sydney、Melbourne和Brisbane等主要首府城市以外的regional locations，驱动力是power、land和connectivity的可获得性。这些新兴市场为运营商和当地社区带来了重大的开发机遇和基础设施挑战。
stories.why_zh: 区域迁移威胁将澳大利亚的data center市场从三个主导的大都会枢纽分散为小型设施的分散网络，使interconnection economics复杂化，并可能降低仍以Sydney为中心的金融服务和实时应用的latency。对于区域经济，涌入代表了变革性的就业，但也使为农业而非工业负载设计的当地电网和水系统紧张，如果基础设施升级被认为是以社区为代价补贴外国技术资本，则会产生政治摩擦。
stories.content:
Australia’s next generation of data centres may not be built in Sydney, Melbourne, or Brisbane. Instead, many of the industry’s most ambitious projects are expected to emerge in regional locations, where access to power, land, and connectivity is creating new opportunities for large-scale development. Yet while the opportunity is enormous, so too are the challenges.

Industry expert, Head of Legrand Data Centre Solutions Brendan Dessent, **told W.Media** that the biggest constraint may not be technology or capital. It could, in fact, be people.

### A workforce challenge unlike any before

The Australian data centre sector is entering a period of unprecedented growth. “Data centre operators and contractors are competing for the same pool of skilled electricians, mechanical tradespeople, and technical specialists needed across housing, transport, healthcare and other infrastructure projects,” said Dessent. “The elephant in the room is staff.”

The challenge becomes even greater when developments move beyond major metropolitan centres. Recent proposals for large-scale data centres in regional areas have sparked broader conversations about accommodation shortages, workforce mobility, and how communities can support temporary construction populations. One example involves a coastal project considering cruise ships as temporary accommodation for workers, highlighting the unconventional solutions that may be required as projects move into less populated areas.

### Regional Australia’s opportunity

Despite the challenges, many see that there are significant benefits for regional communities. Areas historically associated with power generation and heavy industry could become attractive locations for future digital infrastructure developments. Communities that have experienced population decline or economic transition may find new opportunities in data centre construction and operation.

The discussion highlighted Victorias Latrobe Valley as an example of a region with a long history of supporting electricity infrastructure, suggesting that future developments could help stimulate renewed investment in regional centres. New transport links, airport upgrades, and supporting infrastructure may also emerge as data centre investment expands into regional areas.

### Modular construction becomes essential

To make regional developments viable, the industry is expected to rely heavily on prefabrication and modular construction. Switchrooms, electrical assemblies, and other major infrastructure elements can be manufactured in metropolitan centres before being transported and installed on site, reducing labour requirements in remote locations.

This approach mirrors strategies long employed by Australia’s mining sector, which has decades of experience delivering large-scale infrastructure projects in remote environments.

According to Dessent, the data centre sector has much to learn from mining when it comes to modularisation, logistics, and workforce deployment.

### Australia punches above its weight

“The enthusiasm surrounding Australian data centre investment is being driven by more than domestic demand,” he said. “Australia’s geopolitical stability, strong connectivity, and proximity to major population centres across Asia are making it an increasingly attractive destination for hyperscale investment…Perth, in particular, is a location with significant long-term potential due to its alignment with Asian time zones and proximity to a substantial portion of the world’s population,” said Dessent.

The result is an industry that many believe is still only at the beginning of its growth cycle.

Dessent also noted that planned regional developments measuring hundreds of megawatts have yet to be fully realised, suggesting the sector’s most ambitious expansion phase still lie ahead.

### Building Australia’s digital future

For all the attention focused on artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and digital transformation, the conversation ultimately comes back to infrastructure. Australia’s data centres are creating jobs, attracting investment, and driving construction activity at a scale few predicted a decade ago. The next chapter will depend on whether the industry can solve its workforce and regional delivery challenges.

If it can, data centres may prove to be more than digital infrastructure. They could become a catalyst for the revitalisation of regional Australia itself.

*This article, the first of two, is based on a W.Media interview with Brendan Dessent at the Sydney Cloud & Datacenter Convention 2026 in September. **Listen to the full podcast.***

stories.title: SAP & NTT team up on sovereign cloud for governments
stories.summary: Governments and defence operators could gain tighter control over sensitive systems as the two groups target regulated customers with sovereign cloud services.
stories.title_zh: SAP 与 NTT 联手为政府提供 sovereign cloud
stories.content:
Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Today)
SAP and NTT plan to cooperate on sovereign cloud services and SAP Business AI for governments, defence organisations and critical infrastructure operators.

Initially, the companies will focus on combining SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site with infrastructure and operations managed by NTT in selected markets where customers need strong local control over data and systems.

SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site is designed for organisations with strict sovereignty, regulatory and compliance requirements. It allows SAP-managed cloud software to run in a customer-owned or customer-selected data centre, supporting local physical control, data residency and operational assurance.

The approach is aimed at public sector bodies, defence industry groups, critical infrastructure operators and other regulated enterprises that want to modernise core processes while keeping sensitive data and operations under tighter control.

The planned work goes beyond where data is stored. It also addresses who controls the underlying operations and technology in jurisdictions where local oversight is a central requirement.

### Sovereign focus

NTT is expected to provide infrastructure management and operational support, while SAP contributes its application portfolio and sovereign cloud model. Together, they aim to support customers in markets where legal and regulatory conditions place a premium on domestic control and assurance.

The scope also includes examining how artificial intelligence can be adopted in heavily regulated settings. SAP and NTT plan to explore wider opportunities for governments, critical infrastructure operators and other regulated industries to use AI in ways that meet sovereignty requirements.

This work is expected to centre on SAP Business AI, which could be applied to mission-critical processes in organisations that must balance modernisation with compliance and security obligations.

The announcement comes as governments and regulated industries face pressure to update ageing systems while keeping closer oversight of sensitive information, infrastructure and digital operations. Sovereign cloud models are drawing growing interest from organisations that want to use cloud-based software without giving up too much operational control.

In many cases, those requirements go beyond data residency to include assurance over staffing, operational processes and the physical environment in which systems run. Defence-related organisations and operators of essential services have been among the most cautious adopters of public cloud and AI tools because of these constraints.

For SAP, the cooperation reflects demand for cloud deployments that give customers more control than standard public cloud arrangements. For NTT, it offers another route into customers seeking managed infrastructure for sensitive workloads in regulated sectors.

Dominik Asam, member of the Executive Board and Chief Financial Officer at SAP, outlined the companies' position on the planned work. "With this cooperation, SAP and NTT aim to give customers a practical path to cloud and AI innovation while maintaining the control, governance and trust they require," said Asam.

He added: "For public sector organizations and regulated industries, sovereignty is not just a compliance requirement, it is the foundation for resilience, competitiveness and the responsible adoption of AI. Together, we want to help customers innovate while meeting their sovereignty requirements."

NTT also highlighted customer demand for AI tied to operational needs rather than broad experimentation. "Our customers are looking for practical ways to use AI to solve real business challenges and create new value," said Yutaka Sasaki, representative member of the Board, senior executive vice president and Chief Financial Officer, NTT.

"By combining SAP's business applications and AI capabilities with NTT's deep understanding of industry needs and mission-critical operations, we aim to help organizations transform how they work, make better decisions and accelerate business outcomes through AI," said Sasaki.

stories.title: Jacobs warns of gap between energy capital & projects
stories.summary: Only 29% of energy leaders say capital and investable projects are both sufficient, as permitting and grid bottlenecks delay delivery.
stories.title_zh: Jacobs 警告能源资本与项目之间存在缺口
stories.content:
Jacobs has published research highlighting a gap between available capital and the number of investable energy infrastructure projects. The survey found that 71% of energy leaders believe enough capital is available, but only 29% say there is both enough capital and enough investable projects.

The findings are based on a survey of 600 senior energy-sector decision-makers in the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Singapore and Australia. Respondents included executives responsible for strategy, procurement, capital programmes and major project delivery.

Across the five markets, respondents identified a set of barriers limiting project delivery even where funding exists. These included permitting and consenting, regulatory and policy uncertainty, grid access, skills shortages, equipment availability and reliance on other infrastructure systems.

More than three-quarters of those surveyed said at least a quarter of major energy infrastructure projects are likely to face delays or cost overruns over the next three years. For 56% of respondents, permitting and consenting, along with regulatory and policy uncertainty, ranked as the biggest obstacles to building infrastructure quickly enough.

The research also underlined how energy projects depend on assets and systems outside a developer's direct control. Some 57% of energy leaders said the readiness of other infrastructure systems was a major or critical constraint on energy infrastructure delivery.

This is particularly relevant for projects that rely on transmission links, transport access, communications networks, water supply and multiple layers of approval. New generation projects can depend on network upgrades, while industrial facilities and large digital sites may require coordinated investment across several infrastructure sectors before they can proceed.

Fiachra Ó Cléirigh, Executive Vice President at Jacobs, said: "The capital is there, but getting the conditions around a project to line up can be harder. Projects can still stall when permitting, grid access, supply chains, skills and supporting infrastructure aren't ready. Identifying barriers and resolving these dependencies earlier can give investors, developers and delivery teams greater certainty and help viable projects move forward faster."

### Local pressures

While the broad themes were consistent across the countries surveyed, the balance of risks varied by market.

In the United States, 80% of respondents ranked permitting among the top three delivery barriers. The survey linked that pressure to rising electricity demand from data centres, artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing, all of which increase the need to coordinate generation, network expansion, regulators, energy users and communities.

In the United Kingdom, 59% ranked grid or network readiness among the top three delivery barriers, the highest share among the five countries. Permitting and regulatory uncertainty also remained prominent issues.

Germany recorded some of the strongest concerns over project risk. The survey found that 84% of respondents there expect at least a quarter of major energy infrastructure projects to be at risk, while 68% identified supply chain disruption as a potential operational risk. The findings suggest pressure on skills, supply chains and grid infrastructure is shaping delivery challenges in that market.

Singapore stood out for concern over cross-sector dependencies, with 67% saying other infrastructure systems are a major or critical constraint. The survey noted that the city-state's growing reliance on regional electricity imports adds a cross-border element to infrastructure and regulatory coordination.

In Australia, 49% said capital is available but investable projects remain in short supply. A further 61% described other infrastructure systems as a major or critical constraint on energy delivery, reflecting the dependence of generation projects on transmission and related enabling infrastructure.

### Resilience gap

The research also found a disconnect between confidence in the resilience of existing assets and the extent to which resilience is formally embedded in planning. Almost 95% of respondents said they were somewhat or very confident that their critical assets would continue operating during a major disruption tomorrow.

Yet only 36% said resilience is built into planning and decision-making. That gap suggests many energy leaders believe current systems would hold up under stress, even though fewer organisations have integrated resilience into investment and delivery processes.

Patrick Hill, President of Global Operations at Jacobs, said: "There is no single organization, sector or geography with all the answers to the energy security challenge, but there is a lot we can learn from one another. From our own experience, delivery improves when the industry shares what works and addresses dependencies earlier - with governments, regulators, investors and delivery teams working from a collective view of what is needed. That is how energy ambitions become infrastructure that serves economies and communities for decades."

stories.title: LG Electronics posts strong Q3 on vehicle & AI demand
stories.summary: Vehicle and AI data centre orders helped lift operating profit 34.1 per cent to KRW 781.9 billion in the third quarter.
stories.title_zh: LG Electronics 因汽车与 AI 需求 Q3 业绩强劲
stories.content:
Thu, 29th Oct 2026 (Today)
LG Electronics reported third-quarter consolidated revenue of KRW 23.82 trillion and operating profit of KRW 781.9 billion. Cumulative operating profit for the first three quarters rose 55.9 per cent year on year to KRW 4.03 trillion.

Revenue for the first three quarters reached KRW 71.38 trillion, up 9.2 per cent from a year earlier, with all four of the group's main business units remaining profitable.

Growth in its home appliance and vehicle businesses, along with an improved television operation, supported the results. Revenue from subscriptions and business-to-business sales also increased during the quarter.

Subscription revenue, including product subscriptions and maintenance services, rose 8.6 per cent year on year to KRW 760 billion. B2B revenue increased 3.4 per cent to KRW 6.1 trillion.

### Business units

The Home Appliance Solution division posted revenue of KRW 7.04 trillion and operating profit of KRW 259.2 billion. Revenue remained above KRW 7 trillion for a second consecutive quarter despite higher logistics and marketing costs.

Management expects only limited demand recovery in the home appliance market in the current quarter. The division plans to focus on Global South markets, where demand has been more resilient.

The Media Entertainment Solution division reported revenue of KRW 5.02 trillion and operating profit of KRW 146.7 billion. Both improved significantly from a year earlier, helped by higher OLED television sales and stronger demand in emerging markets.

The television business still faces pressure from memory and display panel costs. LG also expects TV demand to decline year on year as oil prices and interest rates weigh on consumer sentiment.

The Vehicle Solution division delivered record third-quarter revenue and operating profit of KRW 2.83 trillion and KRW 190.3 billion, respectively. The performance was driven by continued conversion of its order backlog and growth in in-vehicle infotainment.

Automotive demand recovery is also expected to remain limited in the current quarter. The division said it would continue to focus on converting secured orders while improving cost competitiveness.

The Eco Solution division recorded revenue of KRW 2.17 trillion and operating profit of KRW 87.2 billion. Sales were led by overseas commercial heating, ventilation and air conditioning markets, although profits were affected by expansion costs tied to future demand.

### New areas

Beyond its established divisions, LG highlighted rapid growth in artificial intelligence data centre cooling. Cumulative orders for AI data centre cooling solutions exceeded KRW 3 trillion through the third quarter, up from about KRW 600 billion at the end of the first half.

LG is investing an additional KRW 220 billion to upgrade production sites and expand capacity, including securing a manufacturing base in the United States near major AI data centre clusters.

Partial operations have also begun at its Data Factory, which LG described as Korea's largest robotics data factory. Preparations for mass-production infrastructure for actuators are continuing, while the company seeks orders from prospective global customers.

In AI Home, LG plans to work with global technology companies to build an ecosystem based on internet of things technologies.

### Outlook

LG said it would continue to pursue growth in B2B, subscription and online operations in the current quarter. It also said it would respond to external uncertainty by diversifying its supply chain and improving operational efficiency.

The company also plans to cancel all 730,000 treasury shares repurchased this year within the current quarter.

The latest figures suggest LG's push to broaden earnings beyond traditional consumer electronics is gaining traction, particularly in automotive, subscription services and cooling systems tied to data centre demand. At the same time, the outlook points to a more difficult consumer backdrop in appliances and televisions, where demand recovery remains subdued.

stories.title: Alphabet shares fall after revenue miss, cash burn worsens
stories.summary: Capital expenditures driven by AI will rise significantly in 2027, says its CFO
stories.title_zh: Alphabet营收未达预期、现金消耗加剧，股价下跌
stories.content:
Capital expenditures driven by AI will rise significantly in 2027, says its CFO

\[BENGALURU\] Google parent Alphabet on Wednesday (Oct 28) missed Wall Street profit and revenue expectations, and artificial intelligence spending accelerated its cash burn, sending its shares down more than 10 per cent in extended trading.

Capital expenditures, driven by AI, will increase significantly in 2027, said chief financial officer Anat Ashkenazi, adding that 2026’s capex forecast was unchanged. She said she also expected near-term margin pressure from the use of third-party cloud capacity.

The tech giant reported negative free cash flow of US$9.07 billion, compared with analyst expectations that it would come close to breaking even, according to data compiled by LSEG.

The results reflect the huge costs of the AI build-out, with investors in the sector concerned both by potential overspending and the risk of falling behind rivals by not spending enough.

The quarterly cash burn is an increase from US$5.9 billion in the prior quarter, which was the first time the company went into the negative in its 22-year history as a public company.

Alphabet’s cash burn was driven by spending to boost cloud capacity and fund AI research. It reported a US$7.66 billion operating income loss in “Alphabet-level activities”, which it said primarily reflected expenses related to AI research and development.

The tech giant’s total revenue for the third quarter was US$127.6 billion, short of analysts’ estimate of US$128.2 billion, according to LSEG data.

The revenue miss was caused by Google’s core advertising business that reported US$82.01 billion in revenue, about US$1.41 billion short of expectations.

Net income available to common shareholders fell 25 per cent to US$26.17 billion, and adjusted earnings per share of US$2.67 missed Wall Street targets of US$3.02.

Earlier on Wednesday, Google sought to pre-empt its results and counter the perception it had fallen behind in the AI race by announcing its new Gemini 4 Carbon model, which CEO Sundar Pichai told analysts during the earnings call meant it was again “leading at the frontier”.

## Cloud influence grows

Revenue at Google Cloud exceeded estimates and more than doubled to US$30.71 billion in the third quarter ended Sep 30, but was not enough to make up for the ad-side performance.

Cloud chief Thomas Kurian made his debut on an earnings call, a sign of the enterprise-oriented business unit’s increased influence within a traditionally consumer-dominated company.

Kurian said sales of Google’s tensor processing units (TPUs), which compete with Nvidia’s GPU chips, had become a meaningful contributor to his business unit.

The third-largest cloud services provider globally, behind Amazon Web Services and Microsoft’s Azure, Google Cloud has continued to expand enterprise commitments, supported by multi-year cloud and AI infrastructure deals across cybersecurity, retail and financial services.

Alphabet, Microsoft, Amazon, and Meta are projected to collectively spend well over US$700 billion in 2026 to expand AI data centre footprint, chips and high-performance networking capacity.

While industry-wide supply bottlenecks for advanced silicon and data centre power have persisted, Alphabet’s investments in custom TPUs alongside third-party GPUs have helped expand its service delivery capabilities. REUTERS

stories.title_zh: Microsoft云增长和现金流缓解AI支出担忧
stories.content:
The results signal its hefty AI investments are paying off as wariness about Big Tech spending grows

\[BENGALURU\] Microsoft beat expectations for quarterly cloud revenue on Wednesday (Oct 28), offering fresh evidence that its hefty artificial intelligence investments were paying off as Wall Street grows increasingly wary of Big Tech’s debt-fuelled spending.

The software and cloud company also generated US$18.6 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal first quarter ended September – some US$10 billion more than analysts expected – as capital spending came in below the company’s own forecast and Microsoft’s Azure cloud computing business surged 48 per cent.

That financial firepower set Microsoft apart from rivals such as Alphabet and Meta, whose heavy AI investments have squeezed free cash flow and increased their reliance on borrowing.

Alphabet reported negative free cash flow of US$9.07 billion in the third quarter as capital spending jumped, overshadowing a doubling of its cloud sales and sending its shares down 8 per cent in extended trading.

Shares of Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft rose 2.6 per cent in extended trading, paring earlier gains.

The stock has risen about 9 per cent so far in 2026, through Wednesday’s close.

Its five-year credit default swaps – a measure of perceived default risk – remain the tightest among the largest tech companies, according to Truist, even as spreads have widened across much of the AI trade.

The results also show Microsoft capitalising on corporate demand for AI, easing fears that the technology threatens its software empire and that its AI fortunes are too closely tied to unprofitable OpenAI.

## Nadella’s lower-cost strategy

CEO Satya Nadella has sought to capture that demand by giving customers cheaper options, as businesses grapple with the rising cost of deploying AI.

Microsoft has rolled out a string of lower-cost models, while its new Copilot Cowork agent allows users to switch between models.

“By helping organisations build and own their own intelligence, and earning trust through agent safety and security, we are translating our innovation into growing adoption,” Nadella said in a statement on Wednesday.

## Strong azure growth

“Microsoft’s first-quarter report was about as clean as it gets for a company this size,” said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com.

“After Meta’s and Alphabet’s numbers revived AI-spending anxiety, this is the counterweight. Demand still exceeds supply, the commercial backlog is enormous, and returns are finally showing up in earnings and overall revenue.”

In September, Microsoft said it would disclose Azure revenue in dollars, instead of just growth rates, offering a clearer picture of how its cloud business stacks up against rivals Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud.

Revenue at Microsoft’s Azure cloud computing business grew to US$33.17 billion in the quarter, topping Visible Alpha’s estimate of US$32.84 billion.

Overall revenue rose by a fifth to US$92.28 billion, and an adjusted profit of US$4.89 per share beat an average estimate of US$4.73 a share.

## Lower spending than forecast

Capital expenditure for the quarter rose to US$45.2 billion from US$34.9 billion in the year-ago period, but came in below the company’s own projection of US$50 billion.

So far in calendar 2026, Microsoft’s capital expenditure has been US$118.1 billion, which means it would have to spend US$56.9 billion in the final three months of 2026 to hit its own forecast of US$175 billion given in July.

Jonathan Neilson, Microsoft’s vice-president of investor relations, attributed the lower-than-expected capital expenditure to delays rather than any changes to the company’s underlying spending plans.

“We did see some third-party capacity deliveries that we expected in first quarter were actually delayed,” Neilson said.

Earlier on Wednesday, hyperscaler Oracle said it expects capital spending to peak this fiscal year and next, but pledged to raise no more than US$20 billion in additional financing for AI through fiscal 2030.

Overall, Big Tech is expected to pump more than US$700 billion in 2026 into building data centres and securing the hardware and energy needed to develop and run AI technologies.

While faster revenue growth at these companies indicates their bets could be paying off, concerns over the cost of financing the outlay have heightened over the past few weeks.

Shrinking cash flows and rising debt loads at US tech companies, including recent stress at neocloud company CoreWeave as well as record-high costs to insure Meta’s debt against default, have added to market turmoil. REUTERS

stories.content:
- *Delivered record annualized gross bookings of $533 million, up 35% year over year, on robust demand and strengthening pricing*

- *Accelerated new capacity delivery, with nearly 40% more cabinets planned for delivery in 2026 than initially anticipated*
- *Raised full-year 2026 guidance for the third consecutive quarter based on strong operating and financial performance* 

REDWOOD CITY, Calif., Oct. 28, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- **Equinix, Inc.** (Nasdaq: EQIX), the world's digital infrastructure company<sup>®</sup>, today reported results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

*"Our Q3 results and raised full-year guidance reflect the differentiated position and growing importance of Equinix," said Adaire Fox-Martin, CEO and President, Equinix. "We delivered double-digit growth across the key metrics that drive long-term value creation, including interconnection and monthly recurring revenue, and we accelerated capacity to meet broad-based demand. We also unveiled Equinix Fabric One and Equinix Inference Exchange to enable enterprise customers to run, connect, and orchestrate their most critical workloads. Our diverse customer base, expanding ecosystem, and balance sheet strength position us well for sustained, profitable growth and shareholder value."* 

<u>Third-Quarter 2026 Results Summary</u>

- **Revenues**
  - $2.571 billion, an 11% increase over the same quarter of the previous year on an as-reported basis and a 12% increase on a normalized and constant currency basis driven by strong underlying performance
- **Operating Income**
  - $600 million, a 27% increase over the same quarter of the previous year, primarily from strong underlying operating performance
- **Net Income Attributable to Common Stockholders and Net Income per Share Attributable to Common Stockholders**
  - $489 million, a 31% increase over the same quarter of the previous year, primarily from higher operating income and a non-recurring fee earned in connection with our investment in the atNorth joint venture
  - $4.93 per share, a 29% increase over the same quarter of the previous year
- **Adjusted EBITDA**
  - $1.321 billion, a 15% increase over the same quarter of the previous year on an as-reported basis, or a 14% increase on a normalized and constant currency basis
- **AFFO and AFFO per Share**
  - $1.156 billion, a 20% increase over the same quarter of the previous year on an as-reported basis, or a 14% increase on a normalized and constant currency basis excluding the benefit of the atNorth joint venture fee
  - $11.64 per share, an 18% increase over the same quarter of the previous year on an as-reported basis, or a 12% increase on a normalized and constant currency basis excluding the benefit of the atNorth joint venture fee

Equinix uses certain non-GAAP financial measures, which are described further below and reconciled to the most comparable GAAP financial measures after the presentation of our GAAP financial statements.

Equinix does not provide forward-looking guidance for certain financial data, such as depreciation, amortization, accretion, stock-based compensation and other components of net income or loss from operations, and as a result, is not able to provide a reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP financial measures for forward-looking data without unreasonable effort. The impact of such adjustments could be significant. Equinix intends to calculate the various non-GAAP financial measures in future periods consistent with how they were calculated for the periods presented within this press release.

All per-share results are presented on a fully diluted basis.

<u>2026 Guidance Summary</u>

For the fourth quarter of 2026, the company expects revenues to range between $2.684 and $2.724 billion, an increase of 11 - 13% over the previous year on an as-reported basis, or 12 - 13% on a normalized and constant currency basis. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to range between $1.328 and $1.368 billion, reflecting an adjusted EBITDA margin of 49 - 50%.

- Delivered record annualized gross bookings of $533 million.
- Added 6,900 net interconnections.
- Introduced Fabric One, an any-to-any connectivity service designed to simplify how enterprises connect distributed cloud, network and AI environments, with AWS and Google Cloud serving as lead integration partners.
- Announced Equinix Inference Exchange, in collaboration with NVIDIA and Together AI, to help enterprises deploy and scale AI inferencing workloads globally through high-performance, interconnected infrastructure.
- Launched Equinix Enhanced Performance Innovation Centers (EPIC), a global network of production-ready liquid cooling environments that enables customers to test, validate and deploy high-density AI infrastructure alongside Equinix experts and leading technology partners.
- Completed the investment in atNorth alongside CPP Investments, strengthening Equinix's position in the fast-growing Nordic market and expanding its footprint across AI-ready, high-density data center infrastructure powered by renewable energy.
- Advanced Equinix's leadership on responsible infrastructure growth in Texas, supporting state standards on grid costs, water stewardship, community impact, and transparency while reinforcing more than $1.6 billion in long-term investment across the state.
- Established a first-of-its-kind partnership in Georgia that protects ratepayers by having Equinix fund all grid infrastructure costs associated with its Hampton data center project through a 20-year commitment.

<u>Investor Presentation and Supplemental Financial Information</u> 

Equinix has made available on its website a presentation designed to accompany the discussion of Equinix's results and future outlook, along with certain supplemental financial information and other data. Interested parties may access this information through the Equinix Investor Relations website at www.equinix.com/investors.

<u>Additional Resources</u>

<u>About Equinix</u>

Equinix, Inc. (Nasdaq: EQIX) shortens the path to boundless connectivity anywhere in the world. Its digital infrastructure, data center footprint and interconnected ecosystems empower innovations that enhance our work, life and planet. Equinix connects economies, countries, organizations and communities, delivering seamless digital experiences and cutting-edge AI—quickly, efficiently and everywhere.

<u>Non-GAAP Financial Measures</u>

Equinix provides all information required in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles ("GAAP"), but it believes that evaluating its ongoing results of operations may be difficult if limited to reviewing only GAAP financial measures. Accordingly, Equinix also uses non-GAAP financial measures to evaluate its operations.

Non-GAAP financial measures are not a substitute for financial information prepared in accordance with GAAP. Non-GAAP financial measures should not be considered in isolation, but should be considered together with the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures. As such, Equinix provides a reconciliation of the non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures.

Investors should note that the non-GAAP financial measures used by Equinix may not be the same non-GAAP financial measures, and may not be calculated in the same manner, as those of other companies. Investors should therefore exercise caution when comparing non-GAAP financial measures used by Equinix to similarly titled non-GAAP financial measures of other companies.

Equinix's primary non-GAAP financial measures include Adjusted EBITDA and Adjusted Funds from Operations ("AFFO") as described below. Equinix presents these measures to provide investors with additional tools to evaluate its results in a manner that focuses on what management believes to be its core, ongoing business operations. These measures exclude items which Equinix believes are generally not relevant to assessing its long-term performance. Both measures eliminate the impacts of depreciation and amortization, which are derived from historical costs and which Equinix believes are not indicative of current or future expenditures, and other items for which the frequency and amount of charges can vary based on the timing and significance of individual transactions. Equinix believes that presenting these non-GAAP financial measures provides consistency and comparability with past reports and that if it did not provide such non-GAAP financial information, investors would not have all the necessary data to analyze the company effectively.

Adjusted EBITDA is used by management to evaluate the operating strength and performance of its core, ongoing business, without regard to its capital or tax structures. It also aids in assessing the performance of, making operating decisions for, and allocating resources to its operating segments. In addition to the uses described above, Equinix believes this measure provides investors with a better understanding of the operating performance of the business and its ability to perform in subsequent periods.

Equinix defines adjusted EBITDA as net income excluding:

- income tax expense
- interest income
- interest expense
- other income or expense
- gain or loss on debt extinguishment
- depreciation, amortization and accretion expense
- stock-based compensation expense
- restructuring and other exit charges, which primarily include employee severance, facility closure costs, lease or other contract termination costs and advisory fees related to the realignment of our management structure, operations or products and other exit activities
- impairment charges
- transaction costs
- gain or loss on asset sales

AFFO is derived from Funds from Operations ("FFO") calculated in accordance with the standards established by the National Association of Real Estate Investment Trusts. Both FFO and AFFO are non-GAAP measures commonly used in the REIT industry. Although these measures may not be directly comparable to similar measures used by other companies, Equinix believes that the presentation of these measures provides investors with an additional tool for comparing its performance with the performance of other companies in the REIT industry. Additionally, AFFO is a performance measure used in certain of the company's employee incentive programs, and Equinix believes it is a useful measure in assessing its dividend-paying capacity, as it isolates the cash impact of certain income and expense items and considers the impact of recurring capital expenditures.

Equinix defines FFO as net income attributable to common stockholders excluding:

- gain or loss from the disposition of real estate assets
- depreciation and amortization expense on real estate assets
- adjustments related to unconsolidated joint ventures and non-controlling interests

Equinix defines AFFO as FFO adjusted for:

- depreciation and amortization expense on non-real estate assets
- accretion expense
- stock-based compensation expense
- stock-based charitable contributions
- restructuring and other exit charges, as described above
- impairment charges
- transaction costs
- impacts of straight-lining installation revenue
- impacts of straight-lining rent expense
- impacts of straight-lining contract costs
- amortization of deferred financing costs and debt discounts and premiums
- gain or loss from the disposition of non-real estate assets
- gain or loss on debt extinguishment
- an income tax expense adjustment, which represents the non-cash tax impact due to changes in valuation allowances, uncertain tax positions and deferred taxes
- recurring capital expenditures, which represent expenditures to extend the useful life of data centers or other assets that are required to support current revenues
- net income or loss from discontinued operations, net of tax
- adjustments from FFO to AFFO related to unconsolidated joint ventures and non-controlling interests

Equinix provides normalized and constant currency growth rates for revenues, adjusted EBITDA, AFFO and AFFO per share. These growth rates assume foreign currency rates remain consistent across comparative periods. Revenue growth rates exclude the impact of net power pass-through, acquisitions, divestitures and the Equinix Metal<sup>®</sup> wind-down. Adjusted EBITDA growth rates exclude the impact of acquisitions, divestitures and integration costs. AFFO growth rates exclude the impact of acquisitions and related financing costs, divestitures, integration costs and balance sheet remeasurements. AFFO per share growth rates exclude the impact of integration costs and balance sheet remeasurements.

Equinix presents cash cost of revenues and cash operating expenses (also known as cash selling, general and administrative expenses or cash SG&A). These measures exclude depreciation, amortization, accretion and stock-based compensation, which are not good indicators of Equinix's current or future operating performance, as described above.

Equinix also presents free cash flow and adjusted free cash flow. Free cash flow is defined as net cash provided by (used in) operating activities plus net cash provided by (used in) investing activities excluding the net purchases of and distributions from equity investments. Adjusted free cash flow is defined as free cash flow excluding any real estate and business acquisitions, net of cash and restricted cash acquired. These measures are presented in order for lenders, investors and the industry analysts who review and report on Equinix to better evaluate Equinix's cash spending levels relative to its industry sector and competitors.
