stories.title: Oracle AI World takeaways: making Nvidia envious, and storage... sexy?
stories.summary: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure is discovering itself
stories.title_zh: Oracle AI World 要点：让 NVIDIA 羡慕，以及存储... 变得性感？
stories.content:
Who knew the AI cloud world would increasingly become a pick-and-mix of chips?

After a day at Oracle AI World’s Las Vegas event centered primarily on applications (understandable, given the company’s focus, but nonetheless not where *DCD* gets its kicks), day two of the event saw a tidal wave of chip news thrust upon us.

And while Nvidia is, obviously, still the big dog, Oracle is embracing other chip companies and expanding beyond the GPU architecture.

Perhaps most exciting from our point of view is the fact that Oracle is set to provide access to Google’s custom TPUs (tensor processing units), a move that will make it the first hyperscaler to offer the chips outside of Google Cloud Platform itself.

Why is this exciting? Well, it's just a little odd, but then it's been odd since Google announced that it would no longer keep TPUs as its secret sauce, and would instead offer them to a “select group of customers,” later announcing a joint venture with Blackstone to set up another TPU-powered cloud platform.

One can only assume that a) demand is insane for compute (which we know), and b) Google has stocks of TPUs that it doesn’t have the data center space or power ready for yet, and this will prevent a valuable asset from sitting idle.

*DCD* spoke to Oracle about the partnership, with Karan Batta, SVP of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, telling us: “What I can tell you is that this is not an experiment. This is going to be a cloud gigawatt-scale investment from Oracle over time, and the best way to think of it is that when Google launches a new TPU, we will have it on day one.”

An experiment in terms of commitment to the deployment it indeed isn’t, especially when you agree to purchase gigawatts of chips and do so over many years.

But there is a degree of experimentation that plays into the overall strategy.

Batta explains that in the current context, Oracle is operating in a “very supply-constrained world, but we are also living in a world where costs are increasing, whether it's memory or SSDs and storage,” and therefore, the company's attitude is “the more flexibility and choice that people have, the better decisions they can make.”

With this in mind, Oracle is also negotiating how some large customers purchase capacity in terms of power, signing on for 100MW, or even 1GW of capacity, several years in the future.

“But in three years' time, we have no idea what supply is going to look like. We don't know what the market's going to do in terms of cost. And so you want to be able to make decisions, and you may not know what you're going to put into that data center that far out," Batta said. "So you need extreme choice at that point. Are you putting a high-powered rack? Are you putting in a low-powered rack? Are my needs going to change because I'm having a lot more inference? Are my needs going to change because there's some breakthrough in model training that I need to run?

“So there are lots of these characteristics, not just the workload side, but also the supply side, the cost side, the market dynamics, and so if you already have the power, you want to be able to make those decisions as late as possible.”

Beyond that, there is also the question of power utilization. GPUs create a high-power-draw rack, while TPUs are a low-power-draw rack. With that in mind, Oracle needs to be ready for that reality. “There are all these different variables that you have to sort of put into the calculator and be like, great, I'm going to do this. So, but to be able to do that, we need to be able to validate TPUs and make sure that they work and are available on the cloud.”

The TPUs are well established. As Mahesh Thiagarajan, EVP and head of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, notes during a press conference, “Google is in the long lineup of great technology, but they also come with a different attitude because it's the hardware that actually trained Gemini and partially trained Anthropic. So what you have is that credibility from them, their technology, all this technology, all these data centers, all this network. You combine that together, you reach a new market.”

Beyond Google (and, of course, Oracle’s long-standing partnerships with Intel, AMD, and Nvidia), some more interesting emergents are Cerebras, Positron AI, and SambaNova.

According to Thiagarajan, this is in part due to the sheer level of demand Oracle is seeing. He told *DCD* that everything they are bringing online is sold out for 2027 and 2028 already, and demand for AI compute is “insatiable.” Simply put, the more diversity in chips, the larger quantity of chips Oracle can get online “fast-tracked” and deliver to customers.

But also, looking ahead, Thiagarajan suggests that AI will trend towards more “specialized” inferencing workloads, and chips of the ilk of Cerebras, SambaNova, and Positron, all of which are optimized for specific requirements rather than taking the generalized approach of the CPU or GPU chip, could position Oracle to support those workloads in the future.

He explains: “If you look at the partnership we announced bringing Cerebras online in the first chapter of next year, or bringing SambaNova online, or bringing Positron online. Each one of them has some uniquely different work.

“The way I think about why they actually make sense is that AI is getting more specialized. I think we're in like round one of what is a large wave. People don't understand the TAM (total addressable market) of what we're talking about. The TAM is exceptionally high, and AI is the first phase, and you combine the two, and you look at what the next phase of AI, and what the two years are going to look like, the four years are going to look like, what the six years are going to look like, is we're going to get into these very specialized inference opportunities that actually can bring the dollar down.”

Beyond the chip talk, an area that went mostly under the radar but definitely deserves attention is Oracle’s shifting storage strategy.

The company announced partnerships with the likes of Vast Data and WEKA, both of which offer more intelligent data storage solutions optimized for the era of AI.

*DCD* spoke to Oracle’s Rob Czarnecki, VP of storage & data services, about the subject.

“We don't need to do all that work ourselves. You know, we're not building chips, but we're offering all the chips from all the providers. So why shouldn't we do the same for storage?” he argues, explaining that AI is bringing new challenges to the storage world - data volumes are dramatically increasing, and there are varying attitudes towards storage duration, such as the need for “hot storage” to feed AI models and the proportion that should go into archive, and so on - and there are companies out there that have already done the hard work of finding solutions.

Currently, Oracle is working with them on a software basis alone, as this is the “fast path for us to put this in the customers' hands,” and if it resonates, then there is the potential to adopt the hardware solutions as well.

“With all of this focus on storage and AI and changing usage patterns, it's really exciting that storage is back in conversation, that it's at the heart of this AI revolution. I think it's giving some long overdue attention to some really smart people that have been working behind closed doors delivering the durability and reliability that businesses have been built on, and I think that there's an opportunity for storage to accelerate that AI flywheel and to offer the right options at the right time,” he said, adding that in the future (over the next few years), he expects storage to go through some new iterations and generate conversations.

“I think there's a really interesting narrative on how AI can better inform and manage existing storage systems and make them smarter for the customers. Does that make an archive? Does that pull a cache up? Does that actually need to move? There are a bunch of interesting questions that I think we're gonna see folks really spend time innovating on this over the coming years.”

This only scratches the surface of Oracle AI World, but one thing has been made clear to *DCD.* The world of AI hardware is not just limited to the next generation of GPU; the conversation is getting more interesting, and the problem more complicated. Get excited.

stories.title: Oracle to integrate Google's AI chips into its cloud infrastructure
stories.summary: Oracle will integrate Google's Tensor Processing Units into Oracle Cloud Infrastructure starting in 2027, marking the first time Google's custom AI chips will be available through an external hyperscale cloud platform. Oracle will provide the underlying data center infrastructure including power, cooling, and networking while Google contributes its specialized AI silicon.
stories.why_it_matters: This chip-hosting arrangement breaks the vertical integration model that has defined cloud AI competition, potentially establishing a template where specialized silicon providers distribute through multi-cloud networks rather than exclusive captive platforms. For enterprise customers, it complicates procurement by introducing TPU pricing and support through Oracle's enterprise sales motion rather than Google's consumer-originated cloud organization, while for Google it represents an admission that OCI's enterprise relationships and geographic footprint exceed its own in certain markets.
stories.title_zh: Oracle 将把 Google TPU 集成至其云基础设施
stories.summary_zh: Oracle将从2027年开始将Google的Tensor Processing Units集成到Oracle Cloud Infrastructure中，这标志着Google的定制AI芯片首次可通过外部hyperscale cloud平台获得。Oracle将提供包括power、cooling和networking在内的基础data center基础设施，而Google则贡献其专业AI silicon。
stories.why_zh: 这种芯片hosting安排打破了定义cloud AI竞争的垂直整合模式，可能建立一种专业silicon提供商通过multi-cloud网络而非独家captive平台分发的模板。对于企业客户，它通过Oracle的enterprise sales motion而非Google源于消费者的cloud组织引入TPU定价和支持，使采购复杂化；而对于Google，这代表一种承认，即OCI的企业关系和地理footprint在某些市场超过其自身。
stories.content:
Oracle will offer Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) starting in 2027. This will be the first time Google’s TPUs are made available through a hyperscale cloud provider outside Google.

According to a press release, OCI will provide the data center infrastructure, including power, cooling and networking, required to operate the processors and deployment will take place over several years under the agreement. The TPUs will be used for AI model training and inference, including workloads involving large language models, mixture-of-experts (MoE) models and applications that use multiple AI agents.

Mahesh Thiagarajan, president, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, Oracle, said, “Different AI workloads have different compute needs, bringing Google TPUs to OCI gives customers access to multiple leading AI compute architectures in one cloud. That choice gives them the flexibility to choose the right infrastructure for the performance, throughput, and economics of each AI workload.”

Amin Vahdat, senior vice president and chief technologist, AI & Infrastructure, Google, said, “The next generation of AI will require a diverse range of compute, TPUs give customers a powerful, purpose-built option for demanding training and inference workloads. Bringing Google TPUs to OCI will give more organizations access to this technology and greater flexibility in how they build and run their most complex AI applications.”

Google’s eighth-generation TPU range includes two models: TPU 8t, designed for model training, and TPU 8i, designed for inference. The processors are scheduled to become available through OCI in 2027 although the companies have not specified the initial deployment capacity or the full rollout schedule.

stories.title: xMEMS launches micro-cooling chips for data center component hotspots

stories.title_zh: xMEMS推出面向data center组件热点的micro-cooling芯片
stories.content:
xMEMS has commenced mass production of its XMC-2400 and XMC-4800 solid-state micro-cooling chips, the company announced. These chips are designed to address localized hotspots in AI infrastructure components such as SSDs, memory, retimers, and optical subsystems.Mike Housholder, vice president and general manager of the Thermal Management Business Unit at xMEMS, stated that component-level cooling will become an important complement to traditional system-level thermal management. The company positions the technology as complementary, not a replacement for conventional cooling methods like rack- or server-level systems.
### Addressing Hotspots in AI Infrastructure

The XMC-2400 chip delivers up to 28 cubic centimeters of airflow per second at up to 1,300 Pa of back pressure, consuming about 150 milliwatts (mW). The XMC-4800, targeted for enterprise SSDs, provides up to 48 cubic centimeters per second at up to 1,100 Pa and consumes about 240 mW, according to xMEMS.The company sees enterprise SSDs as the strongest near-term use case. Housholder noted that a cold plate on one side of an SSD can leave NAND packages on the opposite side running hotter, creating a temperature gradient that limits I/O performance. Localized airflow inside the drive can reduce this imbalance, he added.xMEMS builds its uCooling chips on a piezoMEMS semiconductor platform. The all-silicon design generates directed airflow through narrow micro-channels without the mechanical wear associated with small rotating fans.
### Future Applications and Complementary Role

The technology is more likely to be embedded within components than installed as a data center retrofit. xMEMS states that uCooling can be mounted on flex or rigid PCBs and pre-assembled inside subsystems where chassis fans or cold plates alone struggle to deliver airflow.Longer term, xMEMS envisions co-packaging thermal solutions that integrate cooling closer to the processor package. For mainstream data center processors, Housholder suggested that air-based micro-cooling may transition to liquid micro-channel designs due to power density. He added that air-based uCooling is likely more viable in edge AI systems, which have lower thermal envelopes and tighter space constraints.

CDC Data Centres achieved its 2030 net-zero target in FY26, four years ahead of schedule, the company stated in a response to a federal parliamentary inquiry. The target boundary includes Scope 1, Scope 2, and selected Scope 3 emissions.The data centre operator prepares its sustainability reporting in accordance with Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards, including AASB S2, and ensures independent assurance. In FY26, CDC reported an operational power usage effectiveness (PUE) of 1.38.The company also reported a water usage effectiveness (WUE) figure below 0.02. CDC has utilised closed-loop cooling systems since 2007, which continuously recirculate water without requiring ongoing consumption for primary cooling.
### AI Infrastructure Regulation

CDC's response also addressed regulatory implications for AI infrastructure. The company argued Australia’s Security of Critical Infrastructure (SOCI) framework remains fit for purpose, but was not designed as an AI governance regime.CDC supported an ongoing review of the framework’s scope to ensure emerging technologies and business models, including neocloud providers, are covered. This applies where they perform nationally significant functions or support critical infrastructure.The company called for proportionate, risk-based regulation and measures to avoid overlapping compliance obligations. This applies where organisations are already subject to equivalent Commonwealth security frameworks.
### Economic Contributions

Modelling commissioned by CDC in 2026 estimated the company supported AU$2.5 billion in gross value added through construction since 2007. It also estimated approximately AU$444 million in annual economic activity.More than 1,600 ongoing jobs across the Australian economy were also supported. CDC stated community engagement should commence before formal planning assessment and continue throughout a project’s development. This feedback could influence matters like traffic, construction scheduling, landscaping, and environmental management.

A former pulp mill in New Zealand could be turned into a storage-focused data center.

Ruapehu district council this week said it had received proposals for a biofuel production facility and data center campus at the former Winstone Pulp International (WPI) Karioi mill site near Ohakune in the Ruapehu district of New Zealand’s North Island.

The proposals would see the mill turned into two separate developments: a wood pellet production facility by Te Ara Hiko bio-coal, and a co-located data center campus operated by Data Igloo, a firm that claims to be developing “sovereign cold data centers,” focused on storage.

Little information about the data center plans is available.

Focused on backup, recovery, and long-term data retention, Data Igloo describes itself as a “cold data storage business” built in New Zealand for enterprise, recovery, compliance, healthcare, research, and AI training data.

On its website, the company said it is developing a “modular storage campus” for organizations holding large amounts of backup, records, recovery, healthcare, research, and AI data.

“The first campus is specified around a multi-exabyte deployment. As the data grows, the campus grows with it,” the firm says. Full details of what storage technologies the firm would use haven't been shared.

Winstone Pulp (WPI) closed the mill at 1002 State Highway 49 in 2024 after some 45 years in operation, citing unsustainable energy prices, resulting in the loss of 200 direct jobs and more in the community.

News that a wood pellet processing plant could be coming to the former mill site surfaced last month. The site is located next to the Tangiwai substation.

On LinkedIn, Data Igloo said the development “reflects our approach to one of the most pressing challenges facing the global data-center industry: how to accommodate exponential growth in data while managing the escalating costs of energy, infrastructure and computing capacity.”

“Data Igloo is addressing this inefficiency by developing dedicated, ultra-low-energy infrastructure for large-scale globally available data storage, alongside separate facilities for sovereign data processing and compute,” the firm continued. “Compute facilities globally can offload data storage workflows to Data Igloo and free up capacity in existing facilities all over the world.”

Ruapehu Mayor Weston Kirton said the proposals offer the “prospect of significant new investment and employment opportunities for the district.”

“Bringing productive activity back to Karioi is welcome news that could help rebuild confidence, create much-needed jobs and generate work for local suppliers, contractors and other businesses,” he said.
